items.text: Does aggression toward staff (simulated) tend to happen when SIMULATED has been left alone or no adult is paying attention?
Does aggression toward staff (simulated) tend to happen when an adult turns to talk with another student or another adult?
After aggression toward staff (simulated), do adults usually stop what they are doing to talk with SIMULATED or calm SIMULATED down?
Is SIMULATED generally well behaved when getting a lot of attention, or when an adult is close by?
Does aggression toward staff (simulated) tend to happen when a preferred item, snack or activity is taken away or is not available?
Does aggression toward staff (simulated) usually stop soon after SIMULATED is given the item or activity that was asked for?
Is SIMULATED usually calm when free to use preferred items or activities without limits?
Does aggression toward staff (simulated) tend to happen when SIMULATED is asked to do a difficult task or to stop a preferred activity?
Does aggression toward staff (simulated) usually stop soon after the task is removed or the request is dropped?
Is SIMULATED usually well behaved when nothing is being asked of SIMULATED and no task is in front of SIMULATED?
Does aggression toward staff (simulated) happen in the same way across many places, people and times of day?
Does aggression toward staff (simulated) happen even when nobody is around or watching SIMULATED?
Does SIMULATED seem to enjoy aggression toward staff (simulated) itself, as if it feels good, even with nothing else gained?
Does aggression toward staff (simulated) happen more often when SIMULATED is sick, tired or has not slept well?
Is aggression toward staff (simulated) cyclical, happening for several days and then stopping for a while?
Does SIMULATED have a medical condition that might cause discomfort or pain at times?

payload.subject: Parent or guardian questions for Form IN-1

When you have finished, press Send: short answers go in an email to Joshua Newsome, M.A., BCBA; longer ones are saved as a file for you to attach to an email.

payload.instructions: Rate each statement from your own view, 1 (strongly disagree) to 6 (strongly agree), or N/A if you cannot judge it. items.text: The behavior this plan is meant to reduce is the one that matters most to me, or to Sam.
The replacement skill the plan teaches is something Sam will actually need outside this plan.
The amount of change the plan aims for would make a real difference in Sam’s day.
The plan is aimed at the right settings and times.
Nothing important to me was left out of the goals.
The way the plan responds to Sam’s behavior is fair and respectful.
I would be comfortable if Sam’s family, another teacher, or the principal watched the plan being run.
What the plan asks of the adults is reasonable for what it is likely to give back.
The plan can be run in this classroom as it is written, on an ordinary day.
Compared with what was done before, I prefer this plan.
The reinforcers, and the way they are earned, are acceptable to me.

payload.title: Contextual fit, round 1
payload.heading: Contextual Fit: Round 1 (before enhancement)
payload.sub: For a classroom teacher who will run the plan (Break-card FCT with delay tolerance — BIP dated 9/2/26, built on Form TD-1). Do you know it, can you do it, do you believe in it, and do you have the time and backing to carry it out? Rated alone, not in a meeting: the disagreements are what the form is for.
payload.instructions: Rate each statement from your own view, 1 (strongly disagree) to 6 (strongly agree); there is no midpoint, and no statement is skipped. A low rating changes the plan or the supports around it, not what is expected of you. When you have finished, press Send: your email program opens with a message to Joshua Newsome, M.A., BCBA ready to go.

items.text: I can describe what this plan asks me to do, step by step, without looking it up.
I know which behavior the plan is meant to change and how it is defined.
I know what I am supposed to do at the moment the behavior occurs.
I understand why each part of the plan is in there, not just what to do.
I have been shown how to run each part of the plan, not only told about it.
I have practiced the plan and been given feedback on my practice.
I can run the plan correctly when the student is escalated, not only when things are calm.
The plan is consistent with how I believe this student should be treated.
The plan is fair to the other students in the room.
I would be comfortable if this student’s parent watched me run this plan.
The materials the plan needs are available where and when I need them.
I have enough time within the routine to run the plan as it is written.
There are enough adults present during the periods when the plan applies.
The plan fits the way this classroom actually runs, not an ideal version of it.
Running this plan does not pull me away from the other students in a way I cannot manage.
The plan can be run during the activities where the behavior actually occurs.
My administrator expects this plan to be run and backs it up.
I know who to go to when the plan is not working, and I get a timely answer.
Time to train and coach on this plan is protected in the schedule.
I expect this plan to reduce the behavior if it is run as written.
I have seen enough of this plan working to keep running it on a hard day.

extras.label: When you run the plan (which periods)
